title: Next MLS Commissioner Berg Is Ready To Ride The FIFA World Cup Wave
description: Larry Berg, the next MLS commissioner, doesn't plan on sitting on his hands or the league's laurels, realizing the it needs to use the recent World Cup to grow even more.
fullText:
When he was eight years old while growing up in Cherry Hill, New Jersey, the father of Larry Berg saw a poster on a telephone pole about a new youth soccer league starting up.

"We basically had two teams," Larry said. "We played each other every weekend, and it grew from there. I fell in love with the game, and I learned about World Cups. I learned about the broader universe, and I became a student of the game. I became a fan of all the leagues that have been in the U.S. I certainly became a fan of the U.S. men's national team and ultimately a fan of Major League Soccer."

Today, he is more than a fan of MLS. He is the commissioner of the 30-team league.

Berg, 60, was introduced to the media at league headquarters in Midtown Manhattan on Tuesday as the successor to Don Garber, who will step down as commissioner after 27 years at the helm at the end of the year. He will become the third commissioner in league history. Doug Logan was the first, from 1996-99.

Berg, who will divest his interest as co-owner of the Los Angeles Football Club, will be concerned with more than just one team. He has been charged with leading MLS in riding the wave that the 2026 FIFA World Cup created.

"The foundation has been built," he said. "Now it's our responsibility to build on it, and that's what excites me most.

"I didn't accept this role to protect what we've already accomplished. I accepted it because I believe this league is ready for its next chapter. I believe Major League Soccer has entered a new era. The foundation is strong. The opportunity is extraordinary, and I have complete confidence that working together will seize it."

MLS must seize the opportunity for growth on the short and long term. The 1994 World Cup gave birth to the league. The 2026 World Cup can be a catalyst to boost it to an even higher orbit.

"The World Cup this summer reminded all of us why this sport captures the imagination of billions of people around the world. Millions of people across North America experienced that passion firsthand," Berg said. "They fell in love with the drama, the atmosphere, the supporter culture and the emotion that makes soccer unlike anything else.

"For many, it was also their first meaningful introduction to the global game, and that creates an extraordinary opportunity for all of us. The question isn't whether people are paying attention to soccer - they are. The question is what we do with this moment.

"Our responsibility now is to make sure the people discovering our league today become supporters for life. That means strengthening the connection between our clubs and their communities, creating unforgettable experiences for fans, and making sure the excitement generated this summer becomes lasting momentum for Major League Soccer."

While many teams boast capacity crowds, MLS needs to boost its streaming ratings.

When its 10-year, $2.3 billion deal with Apple TV was announced in 2023, fans needed an MLS Season Pass subscription to view matches. In 2025, the deal was cut to 2029.

When the deal winds up in 2029, the league will have to decide whether to renew with Apple or pursue other opportunities.

The deal ends in 2029, leaving MLS to decide whether to renew with Apple or pursue other partners.

Berg said that the next deal will be "finding media partners that want to co-create the future with us."

MLS is one of the few leagues in the world that doesn't include promotion or relegation. And during Berg's reign, he doesn't expect that to change.

"I can understand the appeal for the fan, [but] I don't think it's a great way to build a league," Berg said. "I don't think it's a way to get stadiums built and to get training facilities built and to have owners invest in rosters and all the other things you need to do. So I don't think it's appropriate for our league.

"I think Don has said before, never say never, but I just don't see it happening anytime soon."

During Garber's tenure, the league grew from 12 to 30 franchises. He helped concoct a plan to save the league from extinction when it dropped from 2 to 10 teams in 2001. Salaries rose appreciably. MLS attracted such top-notch players such as David Beckham and Lionel Messi. The former is still playing for Inter Miami CF.

Garber, who will become MLS chairman in 2027, had little doubt that the board of governors selected the right man to succeed him.

"In Larry, our league has found exactly the leader that we need at this time because, most importantly, Larry loves the game," he said. "He understands it because he helped build it. He knows our clubs and knows our league because he's experienced it full-time and understands the opportunities and the challenges ahead. He really understands that our best days are ahead.

"I will say that leading MLS is going to be one of the great privileges of your life, Larry. I think your integrity, your ambition, your thoughtfulness, your smarts, and your respect that you have for the game is going to help take this league to where we all want it to go."

Michael Lewis, the sixth recipient of the Clay Berling Media Career of Excellence Award in 2025, can be followed on X an Bluesky at @Soccerwriter. His 10th soccer book, Around the World Cup in 40 Years: An American sportswriter's perspective, has been published.

title: Ireland's McFerran out of World Cup through injury
description: Distinguished Ireland goalkeeper Ayeisha McFerran is ruled out of the forthcoming Hockey World Cup through injury.
fullText:
Ireland's women must plan for the forthcoming World Cup without distinguished goalkeeper Ayeisha McFerran, who has been ruled out of the tournament through injury.

McFerran's many achievements in the game included being named Goalkeeper of the Tournament at the 2018 World Cup, at which Ireland were silver medallists.

Head coach Gareth Grundie has announced a 20-player squad to travel to Wavre, Belgium.

In McFerran's absence, Lizzy Murphy and Holly Micklem are named, offering them their first chance to potentially represent Ireland in goal on one of hockey's biggest stages.

The side will be making their third successive appearance at at a World Cup, having beaten Japan in a shootout in the bronze medal match in Santiago to ensure qualification for the 2026 edition.

Ireland, who are ranked 12th in the world, have been drawn in Pool C of the competition, and will face Spain in their opening match on 16 August, before playing New Zealand two days later and Belgium on 20 August.

A top-two finish in the pool would allow Ireland to progress to Pool E for a shot at a place in the semi-finals, while a third or fourth place finish would send them to Pool H where they will begin their final classification matches.

Meanwhile, Ireland men's coach Mark Tumilty has also announced a 20-strong squad as the side prepare to make their first appearance in the competition since 2018.

Tumilty has named an unchanged squad from that which secured qualification in Santiago in March courtesy of a comprehensive semi-final win over Wales, before coming from behind to beat France in the final.

Ireland's men are 10th in the world rankings and have been drawn in Pool C of the competition, taking on Australia in their opener on Sunday, 16 August, before facing South Africa and Spain on 18 and 20 August respectively.

As with the women, a top-two place would put the team into Pool E for a semi-final chance, while they would enter Pool H for classification fixtures if they come third or fourth.

title: Cape Verde coach Bubista resigns as Ivory Coast reappoint Renard
description: Head coach Bubista leaves Cape Verde after reaching the last 32 at the World Cup while Ivory Coast reappoint two-time Afcon winner Herve Renard.
fullText:
Bubista has resigned from his post as Cape Verde head coach to join Moroccan club RS Berkane while Ivory Coast have hired Herve Renard for a second spell in charge.

Bubista guided the island nation to the last 32 of the World Cup last month, where the Blue Sharks were beaten 3-2 by eventual runners-up Argentina after extra time.

The 56-year-old also reached the quarter-finals of the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations with Cape Verde, having taken charge in January 2020.

He has signed a two-year deal with RS Berkane, who finished second in the Moroccan top flight last season, and replaces Moin Chaabani, who has been appointed as Tunisia's new head coach.

Renard has won the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) twice as a coach including with Ivory Coast in 2015. He previously led Zambia to a fairy tale title in 2012.

The Ivorians lost 2-1 to Norway in the last 32 at the World Cup and decided not to renew Emerse Fae's deal when it expired at the end of last month.

The former Nantes and Reading midfielder took over the reins midway through the 2023 Afcon - after the Elephants had failed in a bid to reappoint Renard - and the tournament hosts were crowned champions following a remarkable run through the knockout stage.

Renard has had stints with Morocco, Saudi Arabia (twice) and France's women since leaving Ivory Coast in May 2015, and was in the dugout for Tunisia for two games at this year's World Cup.

The length of the 57-year-old's contract has not been disclosed and the Frenchman is expected in Abidjan "in the coming days" to take up his official duties.

Bubista's sustained success with Cape Verde has raised his profile across the continent.

And while RS Berkane, from the north-east of Morocco, are not traditionally seen as one of the kingdom's big clubs they have enjoyed success in recent years.

They claimed their first domestic league title in 2024-25 and are three-time winners of the Caf Confederation Cup, Africa's second tier continental club competition.

Berkane caused controversy in 2024 by wearing a shirt in the Confederation Cup which featured a map of Morocco including the disputed territory of Western Sahara.

Cape Verde qualified for the World Cup for the first time ahead of Cameroon and the debutants proved to be the underdog story of this year's finals.

Cape Verde's football federation thanked Bubista for his "dedication, professionalism, and contribution to the development of the national team's sporting project" before wishing him "much success" in his future endeavours.

Bubista becomes the latest coach to leave one of the 10 African sides which appeared at the World Cup.

Vladimir Petkovic parted company with Algeria, who exited against Switzerland in the last 32, by mutual consent on Monday.

The 62-year-old Bosnian, who was appointed in February 2024, had extended his contract with the Desert Foxes until 2028 earlier this year.

Meanwhile, Hugo Broos stepped down as South Africa boss when his contract expired at the end of July, with the 74-year-old deciding to retire from management.

Senegal sacked Pape Thiaw in the wake of their dramatic last-32 exit against Belgium, with the country's football federation saying it had made the decision "in the best interests of Senegalese football".

The Teranga Lions have been linked with former France and Arsenal midfielder Patrick Vieira as a possible replacement.

Elsewhere, Tunisia appointed Chaabani on a four-year deal last month.

The 45-year-old replaced Renard, who himself took over the Carthage Eagles one game into their Group F campaign when Sabri Lamouchi was removed after a 5-1 defeat by Sweden.

Internal discussions are continuing at the Ghana Football Association after Carlos Queiroz led the Black Stars to the last 32, where the West Africans lost 1-0 to Colombia.

Queiroz appeared to announce his own departure on social media shortly after that defeat.

title: Ireland 'laser-focused' on World Cup qualification
description: Ireland's five-game ODI series against Afghanistan this week marks the start of their preparations for next year's World Cup qualifying tournament.
fullText:
As he prepares to take charge of Ireland for the first time in a five-game ODI series against Afghanistan starting on Wednesday, new head coach Gary Wilson has challenged the side to make their own World Cup history.

Ireland have not qualified for the 50-over competition since 2015 but, as they return to the format for the first time in 15 months this week, Wilson says his squad are "laser-focused" on making it to South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia next autumn.

Wilson played in that tournament 11 years ago, and four years prior when the side famously toppled England in Bangalore (now Bengaluru), so knows well the impact such tournaments have in raising the side's profile at home and abroad.

"We're laser-focused on 50-over cricket right now for that reason," said Wilson of World Cup qualification.

"I've been lucky enough to be part of two and they are amazing experiences."

Stirling returns for Wilson's first Ireland ODIs

Security plans in place for any Afghanistan protests

Ireland are 12th in the ODI rankings and, as part of a keenly debated new format, will take part in a 10-team qualifier next year for just one guaranteed berth at the 2027 World Cup.

Another three teams will advance to a so-called Super Series directly preceding the tournament to decide the final spot in the 12-team field.

Despite the precarious path to even make it back to a World Cup, Wilson does not want his players to limit their ambition to just taking part.

"Irish cricket is really in its infancy in many ways and there's been a lot of firsts within the last 20 years," he said.

"We've had Ed Joyce as the first player to play for England, we've had the first World Cup in 2007, we've had the first Test win, why can't we go on and do something huge at a World Cup? If you'd said 30 or 40 years ago where the Irish rugby team would be now, you'd have got laughed at.

"Whether it's in our lifetime or not, one day we will do something amazing. A challenge I've put to this group is to create their own firsts. I think if we just stay focused, there's something big very close."

Should Ireland meet Wilson's ambitions, it will be in spite of a lack of 50-over cricket. In the three years since the 2023 edition of the World Cup, they have scheduled just 15 ODIs with three of those lost to the weather.

The series against Afghanistan - which Cricket Ireland CEO Sarah Keane has said comes with "moral discomfort" given the treatment of women in the Asian country - will be Ireland's first in the format since a 1-1 draw with West Indies in May 2025.

"It is a challenge of course, but it is what it is," said Wilson.

"We know it's a barrier but there's not any point in talking about it, we can't change it. We have played other cricket within that period.

"Would I have wanted more? Of course, I'd have wanted loads, but that's not to be. We've got what we've got and we get on with it and attempt to beat Afghanistan in this series."

Ireland at least come in with recent white-ball form after June's historic T20 series win over India.

The 2-0 victory at Stormont, Ireland's first wins over the T20 world champions in any format, made global headlines but Wilson is keen to draw a line under the feat.

"More than anything those results probably made people stand up and think and it's something we can try and work off the back of as a wider organisation," he said.

"In terms of the team, we mustn't get carried away with two results. You wouldn't change them for the world, they were phenomenal, but they're in the past now. We must start again against Afghanistan."

Bowler Jai Moondra, the breakout star of the India series, will make his 50-over debut against Afghanistan, while Paul Stirling, who retains the ODI captaincy despite relinquishing the T20 role, seamer Mark Adair and all-rounder Curtis Campher all return to the panel.

title: Vinicius’ Real Madrid current contract details as renewal talks deadlocked due to image rights
description: Vinicius Jr.’s contract situation remains one of Real Madrid’s biggest unresolved issues, with negotiations stretching back to the aftermath of the 2025 Club World Cup, shortly after Xabi Alonso t...
fullText:
Vinicius Jr.’s contract situation remains one of Real Madrid’s biggest unresolved issues, with negotiations stretching back to the aftermath of the 2025 Club World Cup, shortly after Xabi Alonso took charge.

Indeed, as reported by AS, it was during that period that the player’s representatives held their last face-to-face meeting with the club, when an agreement appeared close before talks unexpectedly stalled.

Negotiations are now set to resume from that point.

During that meeting at Valdebebas, Vinicius reportedly made a significant concession on his original salary demands, which had initially been close to €30 million net per season.

Real Madrid also improved their offer, bringing both sides much closer together. Despite the progress, the renewal was never finalized.

Neither party was willing to make the final compromise, leaving an agreement that seemed imminent unsigned.

Still no agreement over renewal. (Photo by Lars Baron/Getty Images)

Vinicius is now seeking a salary of around €20 million net per season, an increase of roughly €5 million over his current earnings.

His existing contract, signed in 2022 and officially announced in October 2023, runs until 2027 and is worth €75 million net over five seasons, averaging €15 million per year.

The agreement was structured progressively. He began on approximately €10 million net per season. His salary rose annually to reach around €18 million in the final year.

The 26-year-old Brazilian also received an additional €2 million per season after winning FIFA’s The Best award, a bonus that would also have been triggered by winning the Ballon d’Or.

While salary remains important, image rights have become one of the biggest sticking points in negotiations.

Kylian Mbappe controls almost 100% of his image rights, a structure that helps facilitate his overall financial package at Real Madrid.

Vinicius is now looking for a similar arrangement. As one of football’s biggest commercial stars, the Brazilian has endorsement deals with 18 international brands.

These include Nike, Apple, PlayStation, Pepsi, Gatorade, Boss, Visa, Marriott Bonvoy, Havaianas, UNESCO, Clear, Rexona, Omo, Vivo, Prada, Dubai Tourism, and Betnacional.

The winger is also believed to be interested in receiving a renewal bonus, similar in concept to the signing bonus Mbappe received when joining Real Madrid.

Vinicius’ current deal expires in 2027, meaning that from January he would be permitted to negotiate freely with clubs outside Spain if no renewal is agreed.

As such, Real Madrid are seeking a quick resolution, one way or the other.

The latest information from the Brazilian’s camp suggests his priority remains staying at Real Madrid by signing a new contract.

Having returned to Valdebebas today after his vacation, Vinicius is expected to hold a decisive meeting with Jose Mourinho and Real Madrid’s senior leadership in the coming hours to discuss his future.

title: Sri Lanka star recalls biggest Gautam Gambhir 'regret' from India's 2011 World Cup final, match-winning six by MS Dhoni
description: 15 years from that fateful day when India won the 2011 World Cup, one former Sri Lankan star remembers Dhoni's match-winning six and his regret for dropping Gautam Gambhir's catch.
fullText:
Sri Lanka star recalls biggest Gautam Gambhir 'regret' from India's 2011 World Cup final, match-winning six by MS Dhoni originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Former Sri Lanka pacer Nuwan Kulasekara still regrets dropping Gautam Gambhir in the 2011 World Cup final.

MS Dhoni's match-winning six off his bowling sealed India's title at the Wankhede.

Kulasekara later played under Dhoni at CSK and admired his calm nature.

Nuwan Kulasekara remains haunted by the defining moments of the 2011 World Cup final, a match in which he was on the wrong end of one of cricket's most iconic images. The former Sri Lanka pacer, now bowling coach of Lanka Premier League franchise Colombo Kaps, revisited the painful memories in a candid interview.

Speaking exclusively to RevSportz at the team hotel in Kandy, Kulasekara reflected on a night that ended in heartbreak for Sri Lanka. India chased down 275 at the Wankhede Stadium on April 2, 2011, with Gautam Gambhir's 97 laying the platform before Dhoni finished the job in emphatic fashion.

For Kulasekara, the defeat still stings, not least because of a costly moment in the field involving the man who would top-score for India. He was refreshingly honest about the part he played in a result that went the hosts' way.

MORE: Bhuvneshwar Kumar breaks silence on India comeback after R Ashwin backs him for World Cup

Kulasekara pinpointed a dropped chance as a moment he cannot forget. He said:

"Yes, at one stage we definitely believed we could win. I dropped an important catch off Gambhir, and naturally there is regret."

"But these moments happen in big matches. Ben Stokes experienced something similar in the 2016 T20 World Cup final before going on to play a match-winning role in England's 2019 World Cup triumph."

But Kulasekara hasn't let these moments sour his memories. He believes such is the nature of the sport. He also reflected on the six that sealed India's win, which he hit off his own bowling. Kulasekara said, "In cricket, especially during the powerplay and the death overs, such things can happen to any bowler."

He continued, "I tried my best to dismiss him, but he still hit me for a six. The positive memory is that we came back and won the 2014 T20 World Cup in a similar fashion. That is how this beautiful game works." Ironically, that wasn't the end of the dance between Dhoni and Kulasekara. The next time the two met, it was in franchise cricket.

MORE: Delhi Premier League 2026: Fixtures, scores & where to watch

Kulasekara ended up joining Chennai Super Kings and played under the very man (Dhoni) who had denied Sri Lanka a 2011 ODI World Cup title. What struck him most was Dhoni's refusal to dwell on that final.

"I joined Chennai Super Kings immediately after the World Cup, but Dhoni never spoke about that final. That shows the kind of person he is."

"He is incredibly calm and always focused on the present. For him, the past is over. His only concern was winning the next game. That is something I really admired about him," Kulasekara said.

Turning to the present, Kulasekara backed his countrymen to compete in the upcoming Test series against India, which begins in Galle on August 15. He said, "Playing at home in a World Test Championship series gives us the chance to show how competitive we are in Test cricket. I believe we can compete with them, especially because we are playing at home."

There is something quietly moving about Kulasekara's willingness to own his part in that final rather than bury it. Fifteen years on, he neither hides from the dropped catch nor the six, framing both as the inevitable cruelties of elite sport, a maturity that speaks well of the man.

His admiration for Dhoni adds a further layer to the tale. The captain who inflicted the deepest wound on Sri Lankan cricket became a figure Kulasekara came to respect at close quarters, a reminder that the game's fiercest rivalries often soften into mutual regard once the contest is done.

title: Chelsea sign notorious World Cup star from sister club Strasbourg
description: Barco, who was involved in a viral heated exchange with Jude Bellingham after the World Cup semi-final, has moved to Stamford Bridge on a seven-year deal
fullText:
Chelsea have signed Argentina international Valentin Barco from sister club Strasbourg on a seven-year deal.

The 22-year-old, who played seven times for Brighton including six Premier League appearances during the 2023-24 season, becomes the seventh arrival of new manager Xabi Alonso’s reign.

A versatile player who can be used in central midfield as well as his regular position of left-back, Barco was in the Argentina squad that finished as runners-up at the World Cup, winning his fifth cap in the 3-1 group-stage win over Jordan.

He moved to Strasbourg initially on loan from Brighton in 2024 but signed permanently a year later having helped the club to qualify for the Conference League.

In all he made 53 appearances for the Ligue 1 side.

He was involved in a heated exchange with England’s Jude Bellingham immediately after his side’s 2-1 World Cup semi-final win in Atlanta, with Bellingham appearing to clip Barco around the head. An unused substitute, the Argentinian had earlier run onto the pitch to celebrate after Enzo Fernandez had equalised.

He is expected to join up shortly with his new team-mates on their tour of Australia and Hong Kong.

It continues a busy summer in the transfer market for Chelsea as they look to remodel under Alonso.

On Saturday they confirmed the signing of veteran striker Danny Welbeck from Brighton, following the signings of Crystal Palace’s Maxence Lacroix and Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Marco Palestra, Emmanuel Emegha and Geovany Quenda have also been signed.

Bhuvneshwar Kumar says he has made peace with life outside the India team.

Bhuvneshwar Kumar has broken his silence on the growing clamour for an India recall, striking a notably measured tone even as pundits push his case for the 2027 ODI World Cup. The veteran seamer, whose stellar IPL 2026 campaign reignited the debate, insists he has made peace with his life away from the national team.

His remarks come days after Ravichandran Ashwin publicly backed him for a place in India's World Cup plans. Speaking on his YouTube channel, Ashwin said, "Bhuvneshwar Kumar is a yes. I would tell him to do all the tournaments - first class, the Vijay Hazare - everything. And get him ready for South Africa. I think we would require him there."

Yet Bhuvneshwar, who last played for India in 2022, made clear that another cap is no longer the force driving his career. The right-armer credited his home environment for helping him move on without bitterness, having been a mainstay of India's attack for the best part of a decade before sliding out of the reckoning.

MORE: Abhishek Sharma scores 233 in 91 balls in district match

Bhuvneshwar was candid about how he has come to terms with his exclusion. Speaking on the RCB Podcast, he said, "I am at peace, and I give credit to my family. At home, we never talk about cricket. We never talk about whether I'll get back into the Indian team, why I wasn't selected, or what went wrong. That played a big role, and there is no regret."

title: Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino is in the eye of a storm after scrapping his attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup. If he goes, who comes in?
fullText:
Life moves fast for Fifa president Gianni Infantino.

It was doing so last month as he was zig-zagging across the United States in a private jet to make him virtually omnipresent as the World Cup reached its crescendo.

On 19 July he must have felt on top of the world as, together with US President Donald Trump, they handed the trophy over to Spain.

Less than two weeks later, Infantino is in a lonely place after scrapping controversial plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment.

Condemned by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, castigated by fans of the game he professes to want to protect. These can easily be deflected as hazards of the job.

Less so the threatened boycott of Fifa competitions by European governing body Uefa, and its subsequent stunning statement in which it declared it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership.

Concacaf (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) also - in their own ways - have offered withering assessments of how Fifa is being run under Infantino.

"This issue extends far beyond a single proposal," said the AFC. "Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed."

Sources say, in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.

On top of that, Carlos Cordeiro, special adviser to Infantino and appointed by Trump as senior adviser to the White House Task Force on the 2026 World Cup, has resigned.

Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to Associated Press that Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project.

BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

It feels as though the walls are closing in on Infantino.

But if this is the beginning of the end of his tenure, who takes over?

Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Fifa leadership

Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan

Firstly, it is wise to be realistic.

Speaking to BBC Sport earlier this week, former Football Association chairman David Bernstein said of Infantino: "In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door.

"But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue."

Former Fifa vice-president Jim Boyce said he thought Infantino would "still have enough support" to be re-elected but "if things continue at the pace they are continuing, who knows?"

He added: "If I was a betting man, which I'm not, I would still bet he will get his final four-year term."

Infantino has been Fifa president since 2016. Before that he was secretary general of Uefa for seven years. Few know the map of football politics better than him.

Now 56, Infantino became president by beating Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. His task was to clean up an organisation tainted by corruption allegations following the resignation of predecessor Sepp Blatter. Blatter was cleared of corruption charges last year.

"I will work tirelessly to bring football back to Fifa and Fifa back to football," said Infantino at the time.

He has twice been re-elected unopposed, and it was expected the same thing would happen again next March. This is not unusual. Blatter was unopposed in 2007 and 2011.

Brazilian Joao Havelange was the last person to unseat a Fifa president in an election, ousting Sir Stanley Rous in 1974. No-one opposed Havelange for five straight terms until he finally resigned in 1998, aged 82.

Letters of support backing Infantino's re-election have been submitted. Will they be withdrawn?

Victor Montagliani (Concacaf president)

Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to, and delivery of the 2026 World Cup, the first to be hosted by three nations. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English.

Explaining his decision to run for the Concacaf presidency, Montagliani told the BC Business website: "Like anything, when I decide to go, I go. I campaigned on my own dime for three months, went to see all 41 countries, from the US to Bonaire, a little island off Venezuela."

Montagliani took the lead when Concacaf hosted an expanded Copa America in 2024 - in an interview with BBC Sport he rejected the idea it could become a regular occurrence. Politically strong, he smoothed relations around Arsene Wenger's attempt to gain support for a World Cup every two years and has never truly bought into the idea of a 64-team World Cup.

At the Leaders conference in 2025, he outlined why he felt football was strong enough to ride out any storm.

"The game is bigger than world current leaders," he said. "Football will survive regimes. Does it cause a headache? Of course. You have to be realistic about that. That is the beauty of our game, it is bigger than any individual and country."

Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa (AFC president)

Initially elected in 2013, he was elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027.

The Bahraini has presided over significant growth within the Asian confederation, through the Champions League Elite, Champions League Two, the Challenge League and the Women's Champions League, which was launched in 2024-25. The Asian Cup has been expanded to 24 teams.

Sheikh Salman signed off the brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure.

Nasser Al-Khelaifi (PSG president and chair of European Football Clubs)

Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman of the European Clubs' Association in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021.

Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to more than 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside.

In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role.

"He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday.

Mattias Grafstrom (Fifa secretary general)

Appointed in May 2024 and an increasingly influential voice around the Fifa table.

Multi-lingual Grafstrom become Infantino's chief of staff following his election as president in 2016.

Another very visual presence at the World Cup, he could be seen as being too close to Infantino - and the general feeling Fifa's next president needs to be a non-European might also count against him.

Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.

title: Soccer-FIFA faces fresh transparency calls after retreat on World Cup sell-off plan
Fifa scraps plan to sell World Cup stakes after boycott threat and widespread backlash
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino is facing considerable pressure after his controversial plan collapsed
fullText:
Fifa has scrapped its plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other tournaments to private investors, after widespread backlash and threats of a boycott.

Fifa president Gianni Infantino proposed the controversial plan in July, declaring that a vote would determine whether or not it would go ahead, but there was anger and concern from many voices in the footballing world.

European football’s governing body Uefa even confirmed a boycott of the World Cup and other Fifa competitions, saying its member nations would not take part if Infantino’s plan was voted through.

The Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which represents 41 nations from North and Central America and the Caribbean, backed Uefa in their stance.

Despite Fifa hitting back in a statement that insisted “nobody is selling football”, the sport’s world governing body ultimately backed down.

The immediate response of some association heads is that Infantino still needs to go.

A statement from Infantino read: “The Fifa Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our Fifa Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

“And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the Fifa Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the Fifa Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

“Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.

“Our purpose has always been – and will always be – to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

“Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.”

title: The Premier League clubs fighting a World Cup hangover
description: Which Premier League clubs have carried the biggest World Cup workload?
fullText:
The Premier League season begins on 21 August - just 33 days after the World Cup final.

For some clubs, that leaves barely enough time to welcome players back from the mandatory three-week post-tournament break required under Fifa regulations, let alone integrate them into pre-season preparations.

Four Tottenham players were still involved on the final weekend of the tournament and may have little more than a week of training before the new campaign starts. Chelsea too were significantly affected.

And Manchester City and Arsenal have their own concerns after seeing more players than any other Premier League club reach the latter stages of the competition.

The World Cup may be over, but its impact on the Premier League is only just beginning.

Tottenham are among the clubs whose pre-season preparations have been most significantly impacted.

Cristian Romero and new signing Marcos Senesi reached the final with Argentina, while Pedro Porro helped Spain lift the trophy. Djed Spence remained with England until the third-place play-off on 18 July.

Assuming players take the minimum three weeks off under Fifa guidelines, the players who reached the final would not return until 9 August, while Spence's earliest return date would be 8 August.

That leaves them with around two weeks to reintegrate before their Premier League season begins at Brentford on 22 August.

However, Spurs confirmed that Senesi - who made two World Cup appearances after being a late call-up for Argentina - was at the club's training ground for the first time on Thursday for pre-season testing.

For managers, the challenge is not simply the absence itself. Players returning so late miss much of pre-season's tactical work, conditioning sessions and friendly matches, creating a difficult balancing act between preparation and recovery.

Manchester City and Arsenal, meanwhile, had the greatest concentration of players making deep runs into the competition.

City's World Cup contingent featured for several of the tournament's leading nations.

Rodri helped Spain win their second men's World Cup after playing 726 minutes, while Marc Guehi and Elliot Anderson helped England reach the final weekend.

Nico O'Reilly featured in England's semi-final run, while Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku both reached the quarter-finals.

Arsenal's numbers were similarly striking.

Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka remained involved until England's 6-4 victory over France in the third-place play-off, while Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino reached the final with Spain.

William Saliba helped France reach the third-place play-off, although he was subsequently injured and did not feature again. Noni Madueke was part of England's run to the final weekend but did not play beyond the quarter-finals, while Martin Odegaard captained Norway to the quarter-finals.

Even though neither setback can be attributed solely to the World Cup, both underline the physical demands being placed on players in an increasingly crowded football calendar.

Those clubs are likely to begin the campaign without having enjoyed a full pre-season with several key players.

The World Cup's biggest workload belonged to Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, who played all 810 minutes of Argentina's run to the final.

Liverpool midfielder Alexis Mac Allister ranked second among Premier League players with 749 minutes, while Spain midfielder Rodri was third on 726.

Several players effectively completed the equivalent of eight full matches during the tournament.

Goalkeepers naturally face different physical demands from outfield players, but the figures underline the extent of Premier League involvement throughout the competition.

With the players entitled to a minimum three-week break under Fifa regulations, for those involved in the final on 19 July - including Rodri, Porro, Zubimendi, Mac Allister, Enzo Fernandez, Emiliano Martinez and Lisandro Martinez - the earliest return date is 9 August.

Players who featured in England's third-place play-off will return a day earlier.

That leaves clubs with roughly 12 days to reintegrate some of their most important players before competitive football begins.

The World Cup has concluded. The countdown to the Premier League season is under way.

But for some players, recovery comes first, and the race to be ready for opening weekend has only just begun.

title: Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan
description: Football's world governing body abandons plans to sell off stakes in its major competitions after widespread opposition to president Gianni Infantino's proposal.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino says he has scrapped the controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's major competitions, following widespread opposition.

Infantino said it had become clear the project had "created divisions" that are "no longer in the interest" of its original objective.

The Swiss official added: "As a result, this proposal will not proceed."

Infantino had offered all 211 member associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups.

Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

European football's 55 member associations, Uefa, voted on Thursday to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead.

Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project.

Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned over the matter, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

That came after two other major confederations spoke out against the plans.

Concacaf, which governs football in North, Central America and the Caribbean - and hosted this summer's World Cup - said its members "rejected" the proposal, with sources saying the vast majority of associations from the region are losing, or have lost, faith in Infantino.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

Infantino, 56, is now under immense pressure as he seeks re-election for a fourth term as president at the Fifa Congress in March.

He said he now intends to "bring all interested parties back together" in the "spirit of shared interest" in football.

Despite rejections from Uefa and Concacaf, Fifa initially vowed to continue with its proposals on Friday, saying "nobody is selling football".

However, in announcing the plans had been scrapped, Infantino acknowledged he needed the backing of the majority of Fifa member associations - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour.

That became unlikely when the AFC joined Uefa and Concacaf in opposing the plans.

Uefa has 55 votes, Concacaf has 35 and Asia has 46.

If all member associations backed the stance of their governing body, that would have meant 136 nations voting against Infantino's plan.

The governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) had said they would discuss Fifa's plan in August.

The governing body overseeing football in South America, Conmebol, said it had asked Fifa for "additional information and clarifications" regarding the "scope, structure, governance and possible effects" of the proposals.

Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, with external investors able to buy stakes in it.

It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

Infantino set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m).

A 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan laid out how Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased payout of 24m euros (£20.5m) per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.

It mentioned "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".

The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".

There was no mention in the document of the women's game.

Fifa said Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time on Friday - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.

The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.

Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat AFC president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88.

Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.

Prior to this week, it had been anticipated Infantino would be re-elected unopposed. Associations around the world, including some in Europe, had already confirmed their intention to vote for him.

It remains to be seen if the events of this week will result in a mass withdrawal of their support.

In his statement, Infantino reiterated his plan was designed to strengthen members associations, "especially in countries where support is most needed".

He added: "Our purpose has always been - and always will be - to unite and improve."

However, the proposal clearly created division within Fifa itself.

Cordeiro, who represented the world governing body on the White House taskforce for the 2026 World Cup, is the first senior figure at Fifa to resign over the plans.

In a lengthy statement, Cordeiro said he "unequivocally" opposed the plans and said he "did not accept the proposition" Fifa needed outside investors to "unlock greater value". He added he had no involvement in the proposal.

It is understood Infantino even left some of Fifa's eight vice-presidents in the dark about his plan, which it is claimed could have raised $10bn (£7.5bn).

Lamour called it "the project of one person" and said "a president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them" but this was "the opposite".

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

In a 15-slide post on his personal Instagram account, Fifa president Gianni Infantino tells his critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about his leadership.

The Times and Financial Times report Infantino's plan to sell stakes in its competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors.

Uefa publishes its first statement saying football is "not Fifa's to sell", and accuses Fifa of 'crossing a line'.

Fifa issues statement confirming the plans.

Infantino writes to all 211 Fifa member associations saying they will receive $40m (£30m) if they back his plans, but that they must do so by 19 September if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).

Uefa says "Fifa cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends."

Uefa's 55 member associations vote to boycott World Cups if Infantino's plan goes ahead.

Concacaf says its 41 member associations also "rejected" the proposal.

Fifa says "nobody is selling football" and vows to continue with the plan.

Asian Football Confederation (AFC) says it "stands in solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, though stops short of unequivocally rejecting Infantino's proposal.

A senior adviser to Infantino, Carlos Cordeiro, resigns citing "a bad deal for football" that would "mortgage football's future".

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Infantino is the "wrong man" to lead Fifa.

Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour says the governing body's own administration has been "deceived" about the project.

Infantino releases statement at about 00:30 BST on Saturday, saying the plan will not proceed.

title: Carlos Cordeiro, a top advisor to FIFA president Gianni Infantino, resigns over opposition to World Cup proposal
description: Carlos Cordeiro called the proposal a "bad deal for football."
fullText:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s ploy to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors has angered another significant party. Carlos Cordeiro, one of Infantino’s top advisors, resigned from his position at FIFA over Infantino’s proposal.

Cordeiro announced his decision in a scathing statement that made clear he was strongly opposed to the idea of selling stakes in the event.

A portion of his statement read:

“As a Senior Advisor to the FIFA President, a former banker, and a lifelong football fan, I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup.

“Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA’s Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game.”

Cordeiro then called for FIFA’s proposal to be rejected.

Later in his statement, Cordeiro claimed FIFA has “extraordinary financial resources” and doesn’t need private investment. FIFA is set to make a revenue around $15 billion for the 2022-26 World Cup cycle, per The Times

Cordeiro also questioned the timing of Infantino’s proposal.

“Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?”

He eventually called the proposal a “defining question for FIFA’s future” before announcing his resignation.

Cordeiro was far from the only significant voice to take a stand. On Thursday, UEFA announced a boycott of the World Cup and all FIFA-run competitions until the proposal was scrapped and Infantino promised to never go down that road again. Concacaf didn’t announce a boycott, but issued a critical response calling out Infantino for not going through the proper channels before trying to push a deal through.

FIFA responded to both UEFA and Concacaf late Thursday, expressing disappointment that the proposal leaked. FIFA decided to put the decision on all member associations, saying they should all “have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries.”

FIFA’s statement declared, “Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain.”

Cordeiro has been with FIFA since 2021. Prior to that, he served as U.S. Soccer president between 2018 and 2020. He resigned from that position after a disagreement with the USWNT over equal pay.

In his resignation letter from FIFA, Cordeiro urged others at the organization to speak up in opposition to the proposal.

title: 'Naturally it's going to' - Palmer says England snub gives extra motivation
description: Chelsea forward Cole Palmer says being told he was "essentially not good enough" to make England's World Cup squad will serve as extra motivation this season. fullText:
Chelsea forward Cole Palmer says being told he was "essentially not good enough" to make England's World Cup squad will serve as extra motivation this season.

The 24-year-old was controversially left out of Thomas Tuchel's squad, with England finishing third.

Palmer competed at the Club World Cup, the European Championship and the European Under-21 Championship before enjoying his first summer holiday as a professional footballer this time around.

He said he went to Marbella with his family but found the experience "strange" at first, admitting he "got bored after six weeks" and was eager to return.

"I never thought I'd think that," he added. "I was checking when I was back in."

Asked whether missing the World Cup would provide extra motivation, Palmer said: "Yes, naturally it's going to. It's like anything. If someone tells you you're essentially not good enough to get in the squad, then you're going to think, 'All right then, I'm going to try to go that extra bit harder'."

The playmaker also revealed it was "nice" when new Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso sent him a message soon after learning he had missed out on England selection.

He also spoke about his groin injury last season, which impacted his form, saying he played on it when he "probably shouldn't have done".

Palmer, who admitted he sought specialist advice over whether surgery was needed to address the recurring problem, added: "I feel good now. The seven weeks obviously helped. I'm ready to go again."

title: Vozinha's Colo Colo move delayed by 'personal matters': club
description: Vozinha, the goalkeeper who played a key role in Cape Verde's fairytale World Cup run, has delayed his arrival in Chile to sign for Colo Colo because of "personal matters," the club's sporting director said on Thursday.Colo Colo president Anibal Mosa had announced the signing of the 40-year-old keeper last Friday, later saying he would arrive in Chile on Thursday.
fullText:
Vozinha, the goalkeeper who played a key role in Cape Verde's fairytale World Cup run, has delayed his arrival in Chile to sign for Colo Colo because of "personal matters," the club's sporting director said on Thursday.

Colo Colo president Anibal Mosa had announced the signing of the 40-year-old keeper last Friday, later saying he would arrive in Chile on Thursday.

The delay fueled speculation in the local press, with some reporting that Vozinha was also in talks with Moroccan club RS Berkane.

"An additional period has been requested to resolve some personal matters ... and we’ll surely have news soon regarding his travel schedule," Jaime Pizarro, Colo Colo’s sporting director, told reporters.

Pizarro said immigration procedures were also a factor in the delay and that the club had accepted Vozinha's requests "to allow him to attend to his needs."

Vozinha starred at the World Cup with heroic displays in a 0-0 group-stage draw against eventual champions Spain and in a 3-2 extra-time loss to finalists Argentina in the knock-out rounds.

The keeper, whose full name is Josimar Jose Evora Dias, will move to Chile from Chaves of the Portuguese second division. Although he did not sign his first professional contract until he was 26, he has also played in Cyprus, Slovakia, Moldova and Angola.

His performance at the World Cup earned him worldwide fame, and his Instagram account jumped from 50,000 followers to more than 29 million.

title: Is Infantino finished? Could Uefa boycott World Cup? What happens now?
description: It's been a seismic 48 hours for football after Uefa threatened to boycott the World Cup and Concacaf rejected Gianni Infantino's funding plan - what happens now, and can Fifa's president survive?
fullText:
The bombshell statement landed at 16:00 BST on Thursday, 30 July.

In terms of impact, European football's governing body Uefa could not have gone any bigger.

"Uefa and its national associations will not participate in Fifa competitions," it said.

Eleven brutal words. The definitive reaction to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a 20% stake in a subsidiary company set up to run the world governing body's competitions, including the World Cup.

A company it is intended Fifa will run but that will be part-funded by private investors, including the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Joshua Kushner.

It feels as though no-one who matters knows how this situation is going to play out just yet.

"Not sure the detail was considered when deciding the overall policy," was the response from a senior European football source when asked what this decision means for the U20 Women's World Cup, starting on 5 September, being hosted by Poland and featuring plenty of European nations.

Uefa's boycott threat will be activated if Infantino's funding deal is accepted.

Given 19 September is the deadline for countries to accept Fifa's deal and bank $20m (£15m) on 1 January, in theory, countries could be pulling out of that tournament in the middle of the quarter-finals and before the semis.

After that, the next senior matches in a Fifa competition are the Women's World Cup play-offs in October, which feature England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland among others.

"Wales is involved in the play-offs for the Women's World Cup in the autumn, and it would be our first qualification for a World Cup," Uefa vice-president and ex-Wales international Laura McAllister told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Nobody can even countenance the thought of not being involved in those.

"But let's be clear here. This is not a problem of Uefa's making. It's a problem that Fifa have created. Nobody wants the players to suffer, and nobody wants nations to suffer when it comes to the most prestigious competitions.

"We've been pushed into this corner and that's Fifa's responsibility."

Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approved

Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?

Uefa threatens full Fifa boycott over World Cup sale plans

No-one can be certain what happens now. And no-one knows what the future for Infantino is.

Fifa is yet to respond to Uefa's statement, which was followed up by another from Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and hosted this year's World Cup, saying their 41 members rejected the proposals.

Yet, in a sense, it is not Fifa's argument.

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt is a Fifa vice-president. She spoke out against the plan at Uefa's emergency meeting on Thursday. The FA said it stands "shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues" on the matter.

Scottish FA president Mike Mulraney is also chair of Fifa's finance committee. The Scottish FA's statement said the organisation "agrees unequivocally" with Uefa's stance.

The repeated responses from those who have spoken out are of fury at the lack of proper consultation and lack of dialogue from Infantino, including with his Fifa colleagues, as much as with the proposals themselves.

"Anger," said one source, when asked for the prevailing mood at Uefa's emergency meeting.

Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. The Swiss is due to stand for a fourth term in March.

Prior to this week, it had been anticipated he would be re-elected unopposed. FAs around the world, including some in Europe, have already confirmed their intention to support the 56-year-old.

But sources say in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.

Now there is talk of trying to find someone to stand against him.

The name of Nasser Al-Khelaifi has been mentioned. This is understandable. Qatari Al-Khelaifi is already one of the most powerful figures in football, not only through his status as president of back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain but his leadership of European clubs.

Previously known as the European Clubs' Association, Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021.

Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to over 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside.

In theory, he would be the best person to challenge Infantino. But he doesn't want to. "He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday.

Historically, sitting Fifa presidents are not challenged in elections. The last president to lose an election was Englishman Sir Stanley Rous when he was beaten by Brazilian Joao Havelange in 1974.

"I don't know, in all honesty," said McAllister, when asked if Infantino will keep his job.

Former FA chairman David Bernstein was asked the same question by BBC Sport.

"In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door," Bernstein said.

"But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue."

Former Uefa chief executive Lars-Christer Olsson told the BBC that Infantino has overplayed his hand and his position could be in trouble.

He suggested Fifa should instigate a reform where the presidency circulates around figures from different confederations "rather than giving people so much power" as it has done with Infantino and his predecessors, Switzerland's Sepp Blatter and Brazil's Havelange.

When asked if Infantino should be removed from his role, Olsson said: "I think that should be a new start for football."

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - Fifa's 'unlikely saviour'

Uefa and PM criticise Infantino World Cup plan

While Uefa only covers 55 of Fifa's 211 national associations, in pure playing terms, it is the most powerful confederation by far.

In the last edition of the World Cup, the Women's World Cup and the Club World Cup - Fifa's flagship events - Uefa supplied three of the four semi-finalists.

If there was no European involvement in a Fifa competition, the commercial impact would be seismic and ensure there was virtually no chance of Infantino hitting the figures he has promised in a letter to the national associations, when he talked about a $40bn (£30bn) product.

David Bernstein feels a solution has to be found.

"I can't believe in the long term that there will be a schism because it would be a lose-lose for everybody," he said.

"Fifa can't afford not to have European nations play in their competitions and frankly Europe can't afford not to be part of it.

"On this occasion, Infantino's got to back down. This deal is not acceptable. It's a friends deal and it's not right. If they want to raise capital, there's other, better ways of doing it."

title: UEFA’s World Cup boycott explained – and what happens next?
description: Is this the end of the World Cup as we know it? fullText:
Is this the end of the World Cup as we know it?

On Thursday, European football’s governing body UEFA announced that its member nations are prepared to boycott future men’s and women’s World Cups.

The dramatic step was a response to plans set out by FIFA, the organisation which runs global football, to sell stakes in its tournaments to private investors. The dispute could have far-reaching consequences for players, fans and the powerbrokers involved.

Our writers explain what is going on and analyse what might happen next.

On Tuesday, it was revealed that FIFA wanted to set up a new private entity — called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) — to manage the commercial operations of its showpiece events, including the World Cup. As part of the plans, FIFA announced it was looking to sell a 21 per cent minority stake in FFE to outside investors. FIFA said the company was valued at $20billion (£14.8bn) by global bank JPMorgan Chase.

Thrive Capital, the company founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is expected to head up the proposed investor group.

To entice its 211 member associations, FIFA president Gianni Infantino said they would be in line to receive $40m in FIFA’s next four-year cycle if they backed his plans. He then gave them just 53 days to support the proposals — or miss out on the potential windfall.

For the plans to go through, however, FIFA needs a majority of its member associations and approval from the 37 members of the FIFA Council.

Coming just weeks after the conclusion of a World Cup dogged by controversy — including extortionate ticket prices, commercial breaks in each half dressed up as hydration breaks, President Trump intervening to overturn a red card for U.S. striker Folarin Balogun, and a surreal half-time show in the final — and following Infantino’s extraordinary Instagram meltdown, the proposals have only intensified criticism of FIFA and its boss.

As soon as the plans became public on Tuesday, UEFA issued a swift and scathing response, saying they “cross a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross”.

It went on to say how “the soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.”

UEFA and its 55 member associations later gathered for a virtual meeting on Thursday, with more than 40 associations speaking out against the proposals. They later put out an uncompromising new statement, saying no UEFA national teams would take part in any FIFA competition until the proposals were shelved.

“Some things are simply too important to sell,” it added. “The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

UEFA taking such a strong stance puts Infantino in a very sticky spot.

There was a call between the 41 Concacaf nations scheduled for today. In a previous statement, it said, “Concacaf was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release. We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.”

The Asian confederation also said it was “disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it through the appropriate and established governance channels”.

Meanwhile the African confederation has called for its member associations to “examine” the proposals in full.

Those who spoke out in favour of FIFA’s plans included Czech FA president David Trunda — although he later performed a screeching U-turn — and Erick Thohir, the president of Indonesia’s football association, who also owns Oxford United in England’s League One, a club who have just been placed under a transfer embargo.

At the 1934 World Cup in Italy, defending champions Uruguay did not participate in protest at the low number of European teams who had travelled to the inaugural tournament they hosted four years earlier.

Uruguay again boycotted the 1938 World Cup, joining Argentina in protest after FIFA awarded the tournament to France rather than Argentina as hosts.

Meanwhile in 1966, no African nation took part in the World Cup hosted by England after they boycotted the qualifying competition in protest at FIFA allocating just one place between Africa, Asia and Oceania, compared to 10 for Europe.

Readers might think next summer seems far enough away that surely it cannot be impacted, but the European qualifying play-offs for the Women’s World Cup take place in October. If UEFA plans to boycott the World Cup, those matches surely cannot take place, as they would be attempting to qualify for a tournament in which they would not plan to compete.

Those play-offs include reigning European champions England and 2019 finalists the Netherlands, as well as Wales, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland and Norway. Thirty-two teams in total would be impacted.

And if UEFA goes along with the boycott until next summer, it would mean reigning world champions Spain and reigning European champions England — both heavily fancied to lift the trophy next summer — would not be in attendance. In fact, six of the top 10 nations would not be in Brazil.

Women’s football will be the most impacted by UEFA’s boycott in the coming months. Four of the next five FIFA competitions are in the women’s game, the first arriving as soon as September with the Women’s Under-20s World Cup, hosted by UEFA member Poland between September 5 and  September 27.

The Women’s Under-17s World Cup, starting on October 17 and ending on November 8, is set to be held in Morocco while, on the men’s side, the Under-17s World Cup follows in November and will be hosted by Qatar.

The second iteration of the Women’s Champions Cup — a FIFA competition featuring the champion clubs from each of the six continental confederations, won by Arsenal in January — is due to take place in January 2027, with the first two matches to be played in the home stadium of a team involved in each match, and the final four games to be played in Miami, Florida.

And then it’s the big one: the Women’s World Cup in Brazil next summer.

But Poland hosting the first tournament to be impacted by the boycott is certainly gripping given they are members of UEFA and would require FIFA either to find a new host entirely or cancel the tournament, given the short notice involved.

No matter how you slice it, Europe has been the dominant force in men’s World Cup history.

European nations have won a record 13 of the 23 tournaments, including six of the past eight, and have provided most of the teams in the latter stages. This summer Argentina and Morocco were the only non-European quarter-finalists, in keeping with a historical pattern that has seen UEFA sides account for 69 per cent of teams at this stage and 71 per cent of semi-finalists.

While the United States have been the most successful side in the women’s tournament, winning four of its nine editions, Europe has rapidly caught up. Three UEFA sides have reached the past two finals, with Spain beating England to win the 2023 tournament.

On the men’s side, a World Cup shorn of Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal, Erling Haaland and Jude Bellingham would be a hollow shell of a tournament. Or, to put it in terms FIFA’s proposed investors might better understand, it would strip the competition of its most valuable assets.

German website Transfermarkt provides estimates of players’ values, and each of its 10 most valuable players hails from a European nation. Of the 104 players valued at €50million (£42.8m; $57.6m) or more, 77 play for UEFA sides. FIFA’s proposal aims to maximise the tournament’s commercial appeal, but without these star talents, the value of the enterprise would collapse.

Similarly, the women’s event would be lacking some truly stellar names. Aitana Bonmati, who has won the last three Ballons d’Or, would be absent, as would her Spain compatriot Alexia Putellas. England’s Leah Williamson, Lauren James and Alessia Russo, too.

In fact, the entire top 10 of last year’s Ballon d’Or Feminin (Bonmati, Mariona Caldentey, Russo, Putellas, Chloe Kelly, Patri Guijarro, Williamson, Ewa Pajor, Lucy Bronze and Hannah Hampton) would be unavailable for the tournament, not to mention exciting young talent in Norway’s Signe Gaupset or France’s Alice Sombath.

It would mean a World Cup without the world’s best, which is hardly what a World Cup should be.

Conor O’Neill and Megan Feringa

Damaging? This destroys it. There is no FIFA Forward Enterprise without European nations taking part in its competitions.

Critics of Infantino’s plan were heartened by the initial negative response it received from the confederations in Asia, Europe and North and Central America, but were worried that the tone of those responses was more “why is this the first we are hearing of this idea”, as opposed to “this is a dreadful idea, just stop”.

And those concerns about the strength of the opposition to Infantino grew when the likes of the English, French and German federations all put out statements that were more focused on the process than the principle.

They need not have worried, though. Because we now know that UEFA and its member associations were just taking a few moments to find their backbones and clear their throats.

This is another European Super League moment. European football has correctly realised that this idea cannot be allowed to gain momentum. If Infantino could have dragged this through to his September 19 deadline, it would have been too late to stop it. He would have had two thirds of the planet, at least, on board. So, Europe has gone nuclear. We will not come to play. And without us, what have you really got to sell?

If this outbreak of unity lasts the weekend, FFE is OFF.

A lot. FIFA is keen to talk up taking football to the world, and equally keen to keep expanding its showpiece, but it remains the case that European nations provide the bulk of the tournament’s quality and, thus, the World Cup’s appeal.

Six of this year’s eight quarter-finalists were UEFA nations, and since money is apparently the main thing football’s governing body pays attention to these days, a quick look at who took home the most in performance-based payments from the World Cup quite neatly highlights how crucial UEFA teams are to FIFA’s pièce de résistance.

After stripping out the $10million all 48 teams got for showing up this summer, and $2.5m in preparation fees, FIFA doled out $223m on a performance basis. UEFA’s 16 teams hoovered up $127m of that. Put another way: one-third of the teams took home nearly two-thirds of the performance-based payments.

A World Cup without those teams would be dramatically diminished.

It absolutely should, right? You cannot with one breath say you are not going to play in the next World Cup but then, in the next, say, “We would still like to host one, though”.

No, if this boycott is to mean anything, it has to be a total boycott. FIFA, its sponsors and broadcasters, and its potential investors, need to know that Europe is off the table if Infantino presses on with FFE.

The funny thing is, some in the game thought it was incredibly unhelpful to UEFA’s cause that the German FA gave an interview to, ahem, The Athletic about its wish to host the 2038 or 2042 men’s tournament the day before Infantino announced this plan.

But then, in the German FA’s defence, it clearly did not know what Infantino had been plotting. After all, its boss only sits on the FIFA Council and those guys are the last people Infantino speaks to about his plans.

Yeah, sure, but only if the rebel alliance starts to fracture.

Europe may only have 55 of the 211 votes at FIFA but it has a far, far bigger share of FIFA’s commercial value because its nations have been providing the lion’s share of the teams, players and winners of FIFA’s competitions forever. Only South America has come close to Europe’s outsized impact and influence.

If Europe stays united on this, Europe wins this row. If some of UEFA’s members start to think they might like $40million to pay off their debts, build their own St George’s Park or hire Pep Guardiola, then Infantino can turn this around.

But everything we are hearing suggests European football really means it. They don’t like the process or the principle. And that mirrors what most European football fans think, too.

Might this view upset those parts of the world that really liked this idea? Those parts of the world that look at the European game with envy and frustration? Those parts of the world that find Europeans a bit preachy and selfish?

Yes, yes and yes. But that does not mean Europe is wrong in this regard. Putting any philosophical objections to “selling the World Cup” to one side, this is not a very good deal for global football. If it wants to go down this road, it could do a lot better.

Some in Europe will also point out that the rest of global football will continue to think Europe needs taking down a peg or two regardless of whether this deal goes through or not, so Europe might as well take the brickbats and be right.

In almost any other business or walk of life, this would be a resignation matter. But Infantino deciding to fall on his sword would arguably be even more surprising than his attempt to sell a fifth of FIFA’s revenues to a group of investors led by Ivanka Trump’s brother-in-law.

Prior to this week’s Infantino brainwave, there seemed little to no chance that anyone would stand against him when the next election for a FIFA president takes place in Morocco in March.

That is not to say everyone loves him — they do not — but nobody believed anyone else would stand a chance in that election, so what was the point?

Is that still the case now? Let us see how he responds to UEFA’s surprisingly strident rejection of this idea.

If he shrugs and says, “OK, I’ve heard you, we won’t do it — it was just a consultation exercise, anyway”, he very probably survives. He has done this type of thing a few times before and bounced back every time, usually with a new idea.

It is entirely possible, for example, that he quickly admits defeat on this one but then quickly comes back and says, “Right, Europe, you didn’t like that idea but FIFA has got to even the playing-field somehow, so let’s have 64-team World Cups with more money and slots for Africa and Asia”. That would be very on brand.

But if he ploughs on with FFE, hoping that UEFA starts to crumble… well, it becomes a case of last-man standing: him or Aleksander Ceferin, and Ceferin has the better weapons at the moment.

That does not mean that Ceferin would be the most likely successor to Infantino, though. For the reasons outlined above, he is not that popular outside Europe and he has not hidden his disdain for FIFA politics very well.

This is why seasoned FIFA watchers believe Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Qatari boss of beIN Media and the president of European Football Clubs, is a far better shout as he spans Asia and Europe, as well as big clubs and media partners.
